title: North Korea’s overseas workers fund the regime – and may undermine it too
gist: A September MSMT report estimates 35,600-101,280 North Korean workers remain abroad in at least 17 countries, earning Pyongyang US$450-800 million in 2025 despite a UN repatriation deadline of end-2019. China and Russia host nearly all of them and refuse to enforce sanctions, while the network is diversifying by sector and geography; the author argues long-run exposure to the outside world could erode regime control.

themes.theme: Scale of North Korean labour exports

insights.claim: The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) estimated in September 2026 that between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers remain deployed abroad in at least 17 countries, a larger foreign workforce than previously anticipated.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Sanctions evasion via labour is larger than assumed, implying weaker effective sanctions pressure on Pyongyang.
insights.quote: estimates that between 35,600 and 101,280 North Korean workers remain deployed abroad in at least 17 countries
insights.locator: A new report (Opens in new window)

insights.claim: North Korean overseas labourers generated an estimated US$450 million to US$800 million for Pyongyang in 2025, despite a UN requirement that such workers be repatriated by the end of 2019.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Labour exports are a major hard-currency source that can fund weapons programmes despite sanctions.
insights.quote: these overseas labourers generated an estimated US$450 million to US$800 million for Pyongyang in 2025
insights.locator: A new report (Opens in new window)

insights.claim: Between 80% and 90% of North Korean overseas workers' earnings are reportedly appropriated by the state or affiliated organisations, making labour export a direct foreign-currency channel for the regime.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Nearly all wages paid by foreign employers flow to the regime, so employers in host countries are effectively funding Pyongyang.
insights.quote: Between 80% and 90% of workers’ earnings are reportedly appropriated by the state or affiliated organisations.
insights.locator: For Pyongyang, the financial value is obvious.

insights.claim: North Korea's labour export strategy has not only survived sanctions, Covid-19 and geopolitical shifts but continues to grow and expand.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Expect continued resilience of North Korean revenue streams rather than sanctions-driven collapse.
insights.quote: It has proved resilient, and it continues to grow and expand.

themes.theme: China and Russia as sanctions holdouts

insights.claim: China hosts an estimated 20,000 to 70,000 North Korean workers in manufacturing, construction, restaurants and other industries, and Chinese brokers were reported in September 2026 to be openly advertising them on WeChat.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Open advertising signals lax Chinese enforcement and potential secondary-sanctions exposure for firms in Chinese supply chains.
insights.quote: Chinese brokers were reported (Opens in new window) to be openly advertising North Korean workers on WeChat, listing their ages, skills, and numbers.

insights.claim: Chinese companies appear to be dispersing North Korean workers in smaller groups across dozens of facilities, including garment and seafood-processing factories around Dandong and Donggang in Liaoning, rather than concentrating hundreds in one factory as before the pandemic.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Dispersion makes detection harder, raising forced-labour and sanctions due-diligence risk for apparel and seafood supply chains sourcing from Liaoning.
insights.quote: Some companies seem to be spreading smaller groups across dozens of facilities rather than concentrating hundreds of workers in a single factory

insights.claim: Russia hosted an estimated 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean workers at the end of 2025 in construction, agriculture, logging, manufacturing, steel processing, shipbuilding and logistics, with some reportedly working in military-drone production at the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: North Korean labour is feeding Russia's war-industrial base, deepening the Russia-North Korea axis.
insights.quote: Some reportedly work (Opens in new window) in Russian military-drone production, including at the Alabuga (Opens in new window) special economic zone in Tatarstan.

insights.claim: Each North Korean worker in Russia generates an estimated $7,500 in annual wages, with monthly pay that can be several times higher than in China, giving Pyongyang strong incentives to shift labour toward Russia.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Russia is likely to become an increasingly important destination, tightening Moscow-Pyongyang economic ties.
insights.quote: Each worker generates an estimated $7,500 in annual wages, and monthly pay can be several times higher than in China.

insights.claim: Russian employers now seek female North Korean workers for manufacturing, food processing, agriculture and logistics, breaking the traditional pattern of men in Russian construction and logging and women in Chinese factories and restaurants.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Russia's labour shortages are broad enough to pull in new worker categories, indicating structural demand.
insights.quote: Russian employers now seek (Opens in new window) female workers for manufacturing, food processing, agriculture (Opens in new window), and logistics.

insights.claim: Russia uses student and other visas to bring in North Korean workers, such as an agricultural complex contracting 50 men and women as 'student trainees', letting both governments keep labour flowing while maintaining formal deniability.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Visa-category disguises make official migration statistics unreliable for tracking sanctions compliance.
insights.quote: This arrangement lets both governments preserve the flow of labour while maintaining formal deniability.
insights.locator: The methods of recruitment are changing

insights.claim: The MSMT, set up in October 2024 by 11 countries including South Korea, the United States and Japan after Russia blocked renewal of the UN Panel of Experts, can document labour flows but cannot compel China or Russia to repatriate workers.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Sanctions enforcement on North Korea now depends on a Western coalition without reach over the main host countries.
insights.quote: The MSMT can document labour flows, identify companies and expose evasion methods, but it cannot compel governments to repatriate workers.
insights.locator: The MSMT can document labour flows

insights.claim: Employment sanctions matter only if host countries enforce them, which illustrates a broader limitation of sanctions regimes.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Sanctions effectiveness hinges on enforcement by non-aligned states, a lesson that generalises to Russia and Iran sanctions.
insights.quote: employment restrictions matter only if host countries enforce them
insights.locator: For Pyongyang, the financial value is obvious.

insights.claim: Hundreds of North Korean workers are reportedly active in African states including Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Nigeria, Mozambique, Senegal, Tanzania, Uganda and Zimbabwe in healthcare, construction and IT, while North Korean IT personnel have been identified in Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam, sometimes disguised as trade officials.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: IT worker deployments create cyber and hiring-fraud risk for companies contracting remote tech talent in Southeast Asia.
insights.quote: North Korean IT personnel have also been identified in Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam, sometimes disguised as trade officials.

insights.claim: Diversification of North Korean workers across manufacturing, agriculture, logistics, shipbuilding, steel, defence-related work, healthcare, restaurants and IT gives Pyongyang multiple foreign-currency sources and reduces dependence on any single sector.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Targeted sector sanctions are unlikely to choke off regime revenue.
insights.quote: That gives Pyongyang multiple sources of foreign currency and reduces its dependence on any single sector.

insights.claim: Despite 12-hour-plus workdays, movement restrictions and group living designed to prevent defection, North Korean workers abroad are exposed to outside societies and information that controls cannot fully block, which over time could threaten the regime's social control.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: A slow-burning internal stability risk for North Korea that cuts against the purely financial benefits of labour exports.
insights.quote: Over time, that exposure could pose a real threat to the oppressive fabric of North Korean society.

insights.claim: For now the North Korean regime appears to have concluded that the economic benefits of labour exports outweigh the risks of workers' exposure to life abroad, though whether exposure produces meaningful domestic change is unclear.
insights.speaker: Gabriela Bernal
insights.so_what: Expect Pyongyang to keep expanding labour exports rather than curtail them for security reasons.
